qs.stem: Which of the following is true about a process in which the rate depends on the concentration? Select all that apply.

options.t: The half-life depends on the concentration of the drug present.
options.why: A half-life that changes with concentration belongs to zero order, where t½ = {{frac:C0|2k}}. A rate that depends on concentration is first order, and its half-life is 0.693 over k, the same at every level. She said: "if the rate depends on concentration, remember our half-life is independent".

options.t: The half-life is independent of concentration.
options.why: A rate that depends on concentration is first order, and the first-order half-life is t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}: neither term contains a concentration, so the time to halve is the same from any starting level. In her words, "our half-life is 0.693 over K, doesn't change".

dC/dt is the rate, and here it equals k times C, so the rate changes whenever the concentration changes: the definition of first order. As she put it, "DCDT is our rate, and this one says that the rate is equal to our K times concentration".

No C appears on the right, so the rate stays the same whatever the concentration: that is the zero-order rate law, the answer to the flipped version of this item ("rate is independent of the concentration": A and D).

list: "Depends on the concentration" describes the rate, the amount removed per unit of time. It changes with the level in first order: {{frac:dC|dt}} = −kC.
In the same first-order process the half-life and the fraction removed per unit of time do not change: t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}.
Zero order is the mirror image: the rate is constant ({{frac:dC|dt}} = −k) and the half-life changes with the starting concentration (t½ = {{frac:C0|2k}}).
Options a and b contradict each other, so a select-all can never key both.

qs.stem: Which of the following is true about a zero-order process?

options.t: The elimination rate is at its highest when the amount of drug in the body is at its highest.
options.why: This describes first order, where the rate is k times the amount, so the most drug gives the fastest loss. It is her key for the flipped version, which asked about a first-order process: "The rate is highest at the top of the curve when the concentration is highest".

options.t: The elimination rate is at its highest when the amount of drug in the body is at its lowest.
options.why: Neither order behaves this way. In first order the rate falls as the amount falls; in zero order the rate does not change at all.

options.t: The elimination rate is independent of the amount of drug in the body.
options.why: Zero order means {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k with no amount or concentration term, so the same quantity leaves in each unit of time however much drug is present. This is the flipped form of her first-order item, whose key was the rate being highest when the amount is highest.

options.t: The elimination rate increases as a function of time.
options.why: In zero order the rate is constant over time, and in first order it falls over time as the amount falls. No elimination process in this course speeds up as time passes.

list: Zero order: {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k. The same amount or concentration leaves per unit of time, independent of how much is present.
First order: {{frac:dC|dt}} = −kC. The rate is highest at the start, when the concentration is highest, and falls with it.
In zero order the fraction lost per hour grows as the amount shrinks; in first order the fraction stays fixed.

qs.stem:
A 165-lb patient received a single IV bolus dose of an antibacterial agent at a level of 30 mg/kg. Blood samples were collected at various time intervals. The elimination of drug seems to follow a first-order model best described by the equation C = C₀e⁻ᵏᵗ. The concentration of the drug (Cp) was determined in the plasma fraction of each blood sample and the following data were obtained:

t (hr) | Cp (mcg/mL)
0.5 | 112
2 | 90.9
4 | 68.9
8 | 39.6
16 | 13.1

What is the half-life of this agent in this patient?

steps.why: A first-order decline is a straight line of ln C against time with slope −k, so two points give k, and the half-life follows from k. The first and last points span the most time, which keeps rounding in the printed values from moving k.
The concentration units cancel inside the ratio, so the logarithm is a pure number; dividing by hours leaves reciprocal hours, the unit of a first-order rate constant.
A pure number over reciprocal hours gives hours. Any other pair of points in the table gives 4.98 to 5.01 hr.
The stem gives no rounding rule. She accepted 4.97 and said a value near 4.19 means "something's funky".

setup.why: "single IV bolus dose" with "C = C₀e⁻ᵏᵗ" and a table of concentrations, so the one-compartment IV bolus block. Asked the half-life, so k from two points by the natural-log form, then t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}.

givens: the earlier point of the pair
the later point of the pair
not needed: any pair gives about the same k

check.t: From 2 to 8 hr the level falls 90.9 → 39.6 mcg/mL, a little more than half in 6 hr, so the half-life is a little under 6 hr; from 8 to 16 hr it falls 39.6 → 13.1, about a third in 8 hr. 5.0 hr fits both.

list: k comes from any two points: k = {{frac:ln(C1 ÷ C2)|t2 − t1}}, the earlier concentration on top so k is positive.
t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}, in hours when k is in hr⁻¹.
mcg/mL and mg/L are the same concentration.

The dose ratio is the other way up, IV dose on top: a larger oral dose would give a larger AUC on its own, and the dose ratio removes that.
F is a ratio of two AUCs and two doses, so every unit cancels: F is dimensionless.

qs.stem: Following a 500 mg IV bolus dose of an antihypertensive drug to a normal volunteer, the elimination half-life was 3 hours, the apparent volume of distribution was 25 L, and the AUC was 86.58 (mg/L)hr. What is the expected AUC after administration of a single IV bolus dose of 250 mg to the same volunteer?

steps.t: AUCIV = {{frac:DIV|Cl}}, with Cl = k × VD unchanged
steps.why: Clearance belongs to the drug and the patient, not to the dose, so the same relation holds with the new dose. The area is proportional to the dose when kinetics are linear (first order).

Cl (clearance) = k × VD, with k (the elimination rate constant) = {{frac:0.693|3 hr}} = 0.231 hr⁻¹ and VD (the volume of distribution) 25 L, so Cl = 5.775 L/hr. The 250 mg dose over this clearance gives the area: mg over L/hr leaves (mg/L)hr.
Her value, 43.29: half of the 86.58 found for 500 mg, as expected. With linear pharmacokinetics a proportional change in the dose gives a proportional change in the AUC and in the concentrations.

setup.why: "IV bolus dose", "expected AUC" for a new dose, so the IV dose-area line. DIV, t½ and VD are given and AUCIV is asked, so DIV = Cl × AUCIV rearranged to AUCIV = {{frac:DIV|Cl}}. k first, from the half-life, then Cl = kVD, because the line wants clearance, which does not change with the dose.

givens: the dose that gave the known area; half of it is asked
not needed for the line; halving it is the shortcut

check.t: Clearance does not change with the dose, so AUC is proportional to dose: half of 500 mg gives half of 86.58, which is 43.29 (mg/L)hr, below 86.58.

list: Half the dose, half the AUC: the expected answer before any arithmetic.
The arithmetic confirms it because Cl is the same for both doses.

qs.quote: What do you expect it to be? Half, right? ... Because we expect for our linear pharmacokinetics, a proportional increase, decrease, or whatever, change. In the AUC as well as the concentration as we change the dose.

qs.stem: The equation for concentration of drug in the plasma as a function of time following a 500 mg IV bolus dose was found to be Cp = 50e^(−0.2t). What is the clearance of the drug?

steps.t: Cp = C0e^(-kt): C0 = 50 mg/L and k = 0.2 hr⁻¹
steps.why: The IV bolus equation is read directly: the number in front is C0, the concentration at time zero, and the number in the exponent is k, the elimination rate constant.

The apparent volume of distribution comes from the dose over C0: mg over mg/L leaves litres. The whole dose is in the body at time zero after a bolus, so it is the only moment the amount is known exactly.

steps.t: Cl = k × VD = (0.2 hr⁻¹)(10 L) = 2 L/hr
steps.why: Clearance is the rate constant times the volume: hr⁻¹ times L gives L/hr. This clearance is what relates the dose to its AUC in the next part.

Cl = 2 L/hr follows from the two readings taken from the equation: VD (the volume of distribution) = {{frac:500 mg|50 mg/L}} = 10 L and k = 0.2 hr⁻¹, so Cl = 0.2 × 10 = 2 L/hr. hr⁻¹ × L gives L/hr, the volume of plasma cleared of drug each hour.

setup.why: "500 mg IV bolus dose", with "Cp = 50e^(−0.2t)" given, and "clearance" asked. C0 and k are read from the first-order line Cp = C0e^(-kt), DIV is given, and Cl is asked, so Cl = kVD. VD first, from Cp = {{frac:DB|VD}} at time zero rearranged to VD = {{frac:DIV|C0}}, because the line wants VD.

check.t: The 500 mg dose read against the 50 mg/L intercept gives VD = 10 L, and a fifth of that volume is cleared each hour: 0.2 × 10 = 2 L/hr, above zero.

list: An IV equation hands over C0 and k.
VD from the dose and C0; Cl from k and VD.
Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per hour.

qs.audit: Stem transcribed from the photograph on page 18 of the annotated deck. Her written working: Cl = k·VD, VD = D/C0 = 500 mg/50 mg/L = 10 L, Cl = 0.2 × 10 L = 2 L/hr. Recomputed: 2.0.
qs.quote: Part A asks what's the clearance, and you should have gotten something like 2 L per hour. Right. The 10 L volume of distribution comes from the dose, that 500 mg divided by RC0.

qs.stem: A 500 mg IV bolus dose of a drug gives Cp = 50e^(−0.2t), and the clearance of the drug is 2 L/hr. What is the AUC of the drug following this 500 mg IV bolus dose?

steps.why: Clearance is the link between a dose and the area it produces: the dose is the clearance times the AUC (area under the curve). Rearranging gives the area from the dose and the clearance, with no plasma data and no trapezoids.
mg over L/hr leaves mg·hr/L, which is the unit of an AUC. The same figure follows from C0 over k, 50 over 0.2, for a one-compartment bolus.

AUCIV = 250 (mg/L)hr: 500 mg over 2 L/hr, with mg over L/hr leaving (mg/L)hr. This IV area is the reference for the absolute bioavailability of an oral dose of the same drug, Fabs = ({{frac:AUCpo|AUCIV}})({{frac:DIV|Dpo}}), where it sits in the denominator because the IV dose puts the whole dose into the circulation.

setup.why: "500 mg IV bolus dose", "AUC ... following this 500 mg IV bolus dose": the IV dose-area line. DIV and Cl are given and AUCIV is asked, so DIV = Cl × AUCIV rearranged to AUCIV = {{frac:DIV|Cl}}. No hinge: the clearance is given.

givens: not needed: clearance is given, so C0 and k stay unused

check.t: AUC is also {{frac:C0|k}} = {{frac:50|0.2}} = 250 (mg/L)hr for a one-compartment bolus, so the two routes agree: 500 mg over 2 L/hr is 250.

list: The dose divided by the clearance just found gives the IV AUC.
There is more than one route to it; this is the shortest.

qs.audit: Stem transcribed from the photograph on page 18 of the annotated deck. Her written working: AUC_IV = {{frac:500 mg|2 L/hr}} = 250 (mg/L)hr. Recomputed: 250.0.
qs.quote: the AUC of the drug following this 500 mg dose, you could take that dose and divide by the clearance that you just found. And you should get 250 mg per liter times an hour.

qs.stem: A 500 mg IV bolus dose of a drug gives an AUC of 250 (mg/L)hr. If the AUC following a 500-mg oral tablet dose was found to be 188 mcg hr/mL, what is the oral bioavailability of the drug from the tablet?

steps.why: The tablet is compared with the IV bolus of the same drug, so this is an absolute bioavailability with the IV AUC (area under the curve) underneath.

steps.t: 188 mcg hr/mL = 188 (mg/L)hr, because mcg/mL and mg/L are the same concentration
steps.why: One microgram per millilitre is one milligram per litre, so the two AUCs are already in the same unit and cancel. The doses are both 500 mg, so the dose ratio is 1.
With equal doses F is the AUC ratio alone. The same answer comes from F = {{frac:Cl × AUCpo|Dpo}} = {{frac:(2 L/hr)(188 (mg/L)hr)|500 mg}} = 0.752.
Her value, 75 per cent. Written as 0.75 or as 75 per cent; three quarters of the tablet dose becomes available for the body to use.

setup.why: "IV bolus dose" against "500-mg oral tablet dose", so "oral bioavailability" is absolute. AUCIV, AUCpo and the two equal doses are given and Fabs is asked, so Fabs = ({{frac:AUCpo|AUCIV}})({{frac:DIV|Dpo}}) with the dose ratio one. No hinge: mcg hr/mL and (mg/L)hr are the same unit.

givens: the numerator of the dose ratio, which is 1
the denominator of the area ratio
the denominator of the dose ratio, which is 1
the numerator; mcg hr/mL is the same unit as (mg/L)hr

check.t: Equal doses, so F is just the area ratio: 188 is three-quarters of 250, so F is about 0.75. F must lie between 0 and 1.

list: Equal doses, so F is simply the oral AUC over the IV AUC.
Either the AUC ratio or Cl × AUCpo over Dpo; both give 0.752.
Fabs = ({{frac:AUCpo|AUCIV}})({{frac:DIV|Dpo}}): the ratio of the two AUCs, corrected for the doses when they differ.
AUCIV is the denominator because the IV dose is the reference; for an IV dose F is 1.
The dose ratio is the other way up, IV dose on top: a larger oral dose would give a larger AUC on its own, and the dose ratio removes that.
F is a ratio of two AUCs and two doses, so every unit cancels: F is dimensionless.

qs.audit: Stem transcribed from the photograph on page 18 of the annotated deck; the sheet prints the oral AUC as "188 mcg hr/mL" while part (b) is in (mg/L)hr, and the two units are equal. Her written working: F = (188 mg·hr/L)(2 L/hr)/500 mg = 0.752. Recomputed: 0.752.
qs.quote: so then the F would be, since the doses are the same, 188 divided by 250, you should get 75%.

qs.stem: 1. A drug with an elimination half-life of 3 hours, apparent volume of distribution of 25 L, and minimum effective concentration of 1.2 mcg/mL is to be administered as a single 250 mg IV bolus dose. a. What is the duration of action of this dose?

steps.why: 1 mcg/mL equals 1 mg/L, because multiplying top and bottom by 1000 turns mcg into mg and mL into L. With the dose in mg and the volume in L, the ratio inside the logarithm has no units.
The stem gives the half-life, not k, so the half-life form of the duration line applies directly; 1.44 is 1 ÷ 0.693, the step from k to t½.
VD × Ceff = 30 mg is the amount in the body when the level is at the MEC. The dose is 8.33 times that, and ln 8.333 = 2.120.
4.32 × 2.120 = 9.16 hr. With k = 0.231 hr⁻¹ in place of 1.44 t½ the result is 9.18 hr; the 1.44 is rounded, so the two forms differ only in the second decimal.

setup.why: "Duration of action" of a "single 250 mg IV bolus", with the half-life, VD and MEC given: the half-life form of the duration line, used without first finding k.

check.t: 250 mg is 8.333 times the 30 mg at the MEC, between 2 to the 3rd and 2 to the 4th, so teff is 3 to 4 half-lives of 3 hr: 9.16 hr.

list: teff: the time one IV bolus keeps the plasma level at or above Ceff, the minimum effective concentration.
From C = C0e^(−kt) with C = Ceff: teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}}, where C0 = {{frac:D0|VD}}, the level just after the bolus.
With k = {{frac:0.693|t½}}: teff = 1.44 t½ ln({{frac:D0|VD × Ceff}}); 1.44 is {{frac:1|0.693}}.
The dose is inside the logarithm, so doubling it adds {{frac:ln 2|k}}, one half-life, to teff; it does not double teff.
Built for a single IV bolus, a one-compartment open model and first-order elimination.

qs.note: Her working gives 9.15; the 1.44 t½ form gives 9.16 hr and k = 0.231 hr⁻¹ gives 9.18 hr. All three are within the margin.

qs.stem: 1. A drug with an elimination half-life of 3 hours, apparent volume of distribution of 25 L, and minimum effective concentration of 1.2 mcg/mL is to be administered as a single 250 mg IV bolus dose. b. What dose would yield a duration of action of 12 hours?

steps.t: k = {{frac:0.693|3 hr}} = 0.231 hr⁻¹; Ceff = 1.2 mcg/mL = 1.2 mg/L
steps.why: The dose line has k in its exponent, so the 3-hour half-life is turned into k first. 1 mcg/mL equals 1 mg/L, so the MEC is 1.2 mg/L.

steps.t: Ceff = {{frac:D0|VD}} e^(−k teff), so D0 = Ceff × VD × e^(k teff)
steps.why: C = C0e^(−kt) with C0 = D0 over VD, written at the moment the level reaches the MEC, 12 hours after the dose, then solved for the dose.
mg/L × L leaves mg: 30 mg is the amount in the body at the MEC. kt = 0.231 hr⁻¹ × 12 hr = 2.772 has no units, and the dose must be e^2.772 = 15.99 times that 30 mg.
Her value is 479.72 mg. 12 hours is 4 half-lives of 3 hr, and 2 to the 4th is 16, so the dose is about 16 times the 30 mg at the MEC.

setup.why: "What dose would yield a duration of action of 12 hours": the dose line D0 = Ceff × VD × e^(k teff), with k from the half-life first.

givens: the target duration, in the exponent

check.t: 12 hours is 4 half-lives of 3 hr, so the dose is about 2 to the 4th, 16, times the 30 mg at the MEC: 479.7 mg, above the 250 mg of part a.

teach.h: The dose for a target duration
list: Ceff = {{frac:D0|VD}} e^(−k teff), rearranged: D0 = Ceff × VD × e^(k teff).
The target time is in the exponent, so each extra half-life of duration doubles the dose.
Check: put the dose back into teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}} and the target time returns.

qs.stem: 2. The equation for concentration of drug in the plasma as a function of time following a 500 mg IV bolus dose was found to be: Cp = 50e^(−0.2t) a. What is the duration of action of a single 500 mg IV bolus dose if the minimum effective concentration is 5 mcg/mL?

steps.t: From Cp = 50e^(−0.2t): C0 = 50 mg/L and k = 0.2 hr⁻¹; VD = {{frac:500 mg|50 mg/L}} = 10 L
steps.why: An IV bolus equation reads as C = C0e^(−kt): the number in front is C0 and the exponent carries k. VD is the dose over C0.
1 mcg/mL equals 1 mg/L, because multiplying top and bottom by 1000 turns mcg into mg and mL into L; the MEC can then be set against C0 = 50 mg/L directly.

steps.t: teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}} = {{frac:ln(50 ÷ 5)|0.2 hr⁻¹}} = {{frac:ln 10|0.2}} = {{frac:2.303|0.2 hr⁻¹}} = 11.51 hr
steps.why: The level has to fall tenfold, from 50 to 5 mg/L. With k read off the equation the natural-log form needs no half-life.
The half-life form gives 1.44 (3.465 hr) ln 10 = 11.49 hr, because 1.44 is rounded from 1 ÷ 0.693; both are the same answer within the margin.

setup.why: "Duration of action" of the 500 mg bolus whose equation gives C0 = 50 and k = 0.2: the natural-log duration line, with C0 read off the equation.

givens: mg/L, the coefficient of the equation

check.t: The level must fall tenfold, between 2 to the 3rd and 2 to the 4th, so teff is 3 to 4 half-lives of 3.465 hr: 11.51 hr.

list: teff: the time one IV bolus keeps the plasma level at or above Ceff, the minimum effective concentration.
From C = C0e^(−kt) with C = Ceff: teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}}, where C0 = {{frac:D0|VD}}, the level just after the bolus.
With k = {{frac:0.693|t½}}: teff = 1.44 t½ ln({{frac:D0|VD × Ceff}}); 1.44 is {{frac:1|0.693}}.
The dose is inside the logarithm, so doubling it adds {{frac:ln 2|k}}, one half-life, to teff; it does not double teff.
Built for a single IV bolus, a one-compartment open model and first-order elimination.

qs.note: Her working stops at t½ = 3.465 hr, VD = 10 L and the 1.44 t½ set-up; this answer is worked from her stem by that set-up.

qs.stem: 2. The equation for concentration of drug in the plasma as a function of time following a 500 mg IV bolus dose was found to be: Cp = 50e^(−0.2t) b. What dose would double the duration of action found in part a? (Part a: minimum effective concentration 5 mcg/mL; duration of action 11.51 hr.)

steps.t: Target teff = 2 × 11.513 hr = 23.03 hr; VD = {{frac:500 mg|50 mg/L}} = 10 L; k = 0.2 hr⁻¹
steps.why: Doubling the duration means the level must still be at the MEC 23.03 hours after the dose; part a unrounded is 11.513 hr. VD and k come from the equation and do not change with the dose.
C = C0e^(−kt) solved for the dose at the moment the level reaches Ceff. 5 mcg/mL is 5 mg/L, and mg/L × L leaves 50 mg, the amount in the body at the MEC.
At 500 mg the level falls tenfold over 11.51 hr; over twice the time it must fall tenfold twice, a hundredfold, so C0 must be 100 × 5 = 500 mg/L.

steps.t: D0 = 5000 mg (5 g), ten times the 500 mg dose
steps.why: Doubling the duration took ten times the dose, not twice it, because the duration grows with the logarithm of the dose.

setup.why: "What dose would double the duration": the target is twice 11.51 hr, so the dose line D0 = Ceff × VD × e^(k teff), with VD and k read off the equation.

givens: mg/L; 500 mg over 50 mg/L gives VD = 10 L

check.t: Twice the duration needs the tenfold fall twice over, a hundredfold, so the dose is 100 times the 50 mg at the MEC: 5000 mg, ten times 500 mg.

teach.h: The dose for a target duration
list: Ceff = {{frac:D0|VD}} e^(−k teff), rearranged: D0 = Ceff × VD × e^(k teff).
The target time is in the exponent, so each extra half-life of duration doubles the dose.
Check: put the dose back into teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}} and the target time returns.

qs.note: Left unworked on the activity sheet; this answer is worked from her stem by the dose line she uses in problem 1b.

qs.stem: 2. The equation for concentration of drug in the plasma as a function of time following a 500 mg IV bolus dose was found to be: Cp = 50e^(−0.2t) c. What is the expected change in the duration of action following a single 250 mg IV bolus dose instead of the 500 mg IV bolus dose? (Part a: minimum effective concentration 5 mcg/mL; duration of action 11.51 hr. Give the size of the change.)

steps.why: VD = 10 L from part a does not change with the dose, so half the dose gives half of C0, 25 mg/L. The level then has to fall only fivefold to reach the MEC of 5 mg/L.
Halving the dose takes away one doubling, and each doubling adds one half-life of duration: t½ = {{frac:0.693|0.2 hr⁻¹}} = 3.47 hr.

steps.t: The duration is 3.47 hr shorter, one half-life
steps.why: −3.466 hr is 3.47 hr shorter to two decimal places: a decrease of one half-life, whatever the starting duration; it is not half of 11.51 hr.

setup.why: "Expected change in the duration" when the dose is halved: in teff = 1.44 t½ ln of the dose ratio, halving D0 removes ln 2, one half-life, from teff.

givens: half of 500 mg, so one doubling less

check.t: Half the dose removes one half-life, 3.466 hr, from 11.513 hr, leaving 8.047 hr: shorter, but not halved.

list: teff: the time one IV bolus keeps the plasma level at or above Ceff, the minimum effective concentration.
From C = C0e^(−kt) with C = Ceff: teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}}, where C0 = {{frac:D0|VD}}, the level just after the bolus.
With k = {{frac:0.693|t½}}: teff = 1.44 t½ ln({{frac:D0|VD × Ceff}}); 1.44 is {{frac:1|0.693}}.
The dose is inside the logarithm, so doubling it adds {{frac:ln 2|k}}, one half-life, to teff; it does not double teff.
Built for a single IV bolus, a one-compartment open model and first-order elimination.

qs.note: Keyed as the size of the change; the duration falls, from 11.51 hr to 8.05 hr. Left unworked on the activity sheet; worked from her stem.

qs.stem: After receiving a drug that displays nonlinear kinetics at a dose of 6 mg/kg/day for some time, the steady-state plasma concentration in a 72 kg patient was determined to be 10 mg/L. Since this concentration was lower than the desired steady-state concentration, the dose was increased to 8 mg/kg/day. This dose increase resulted in a steady-state plasma concentration of 20 mg/L, which was greater than the desired steady-state concentration. Calculate Vmax, KM, and a dose rate that should achieve a steady-state plasma concentration of 15 mg/L. Part a: calculate KM.

steps.t: KM = {{frac:R2 − R1|(R1/C1) − (R2/C2)}}, with R1 = 6 mg/kg/day, C1 = 10 mg/L, R2 = 8 mg/kg/day, C2 = 20 mg/L
steps.why: Two dose rates in the same patient, each at steady state, share one Vmax and one KM, so the two dose-rate lines combine into this direct-method line for KM.
Each R divided by its own C. The bottom is the earlier rate over its concentration minus the later one, which keeps the result positive. The mg/kg/day cancel and mg/L moves to the top.
KM comes out in concentration units, mg/L, as it must: it is compared with plasma concentrations, so a KM in mg/kg/day signals the units were not cancelled.

setup.why: "a dose of 6 mg/kg/day" giving "10 mg/L", then "8 mg/kg/day" giving "20 mg/L": two rates and two steady states in one patient, so the direct method for KM.

givens: steady state on the first rate
steady state on the second rate

check.t: A one-third rise in dose doubled the concentration, so the drug is near saturation; KM is a concentration, here equal to the lower measured level: 10 mg/L.

list: Two dose rates in the same patient, each with the steady-state concentration it produced: KM = {{frac:R2 − R1|(R1/C1) − (R2/C2)}}.
The rate units cancel, so KM is a concentration, mg/L.
Then Vmax = {{frac:R(KM + Css)|Css}} with either pair; both pairs give the same Vmax.

qs.stem: After receiving a drug that displays nonlinear kinetics at a dose of 6 mg/kg/day for some time, the steady-state plasma concentration in a 72 kg patient was determined to be 10 mg/L. Since this concentration was lower than the desired steady-state concentration, the dose was increased to 8 mg/kg/day. This dose increase resulted in a steady-state plasma concentration of 20 mg/L, which was greater than the desired steady-state concentration. Calculate Vmax, KM, and a dose rate that should achieve a steady-state plasma concentration of 15 mg/L. Part b: calculate Vmax. (Part a: KM = 10 mg/L.)

steps.why: The dose-rate line R = Vmax × Css over (KM + Css), multiplied through by (KM + Css) and divided by Css. Any one dose rate with its own steady-state concentration will do.
The second pair, 8 mg/kg/day with 20 mg/L. mg/L cancels and Vmax keeps the units of R, mg/kg/day, because the doses were given per kilogram.

The first pair, 6 mg/kg/day with 10 mg/L, gives the same 12 mg/kg/day, as it must: both rates come from the same patient with one Vmax. Mixing one pair's R with the other pair's Css gives a wrong value.

setup.why: "Calculate Vmax" once KM is known: the dose-rate line solved for Vmax with either dose rate and its steady-state concentration.

givens: from part a, added to Css

check.t: Vmax must exceed both dose rates, because each produced a finite steady state: 12 is above 8 mg/kg/day.

list: Two dose rates in the same patient, each with the steady-state concentration it produced: KM = {{frac:R2 − R1|(R1/C1) − (R2/C2)}}.
The rate units cancel, so KM is a concentration, mg/L.
Then Vmax = {{frac:R(KM + Css)|Css}} with either pair; both pairs give the same Vmax.

qs.stem: After receiving a drug that displays nonlinear kinetics at a dose of 6 mg/kg/day for some time, the steady-state plasma concentration in a 72 kg patient was determined to be 10 mg/L. Since this concentration was lower than the desired steady-state concentration, the dose was increased to 8 mg/kg/day. This dose increase resulted in a steady-state plasma concentration of 20 mg/L, which was greater than the desired steady-state concentration. Calculate Vmax, KM, and a dose rate that should achieve a steady-state plasma concentration of 15 mg/L. Part c: calculate the dose rate, in mg/day, that should achieve 15 mg/L. (Part a: KM = 10 mg/L; part b: Vmax = 12 mg/kg/day.)

steps.why: With Vmax and KM now known for this patient, the dose-rate line gives the daily rate that holds the steady state at the target of 15 mg/L.
mg/L cancels and R is per kilogram, because Vmax is. 7.2 mg/kg/day sits between the 6 and 8 mg/kg/day rates, as 15 mg/L sits between 10 and 20 mg/L.
The 72 kg weight turns the per-kilogram rate into a daily dose for this patient. The weight is used only here; KM and Vmax were found without it.

steps.t: R = 518.4 mg/day, about 520 mg/day to the nearest 10
steps.why: 518.4 mg/day is accepted as it stands. When a stem asks for the nearest 10, and also for the nearest 5, it becomes 520 mg/day.

setup.why: "a dose rate that should achieve a steady-state plasma concentration of 15 mg/L": the dose-rate line with the KM and Vmax of parts a and b, then times 72 kg.

check.t: 15 mg/L lies between 10 and 20 mg/L, so the rate must lie between 6 and 8 mg/kg/day: 7.2 mg/kg/day, or 518.4 mg/day for 72 kg.

list: R = {{frac:Vmax × Css|KM + Css}}. R is the dose rate, an amount per unit time; Vmax (maximum elimination rate) has the units of R; KM (Michaelis constant) and Css are concentrations.

Report a dose rate, such as mg/day, not an amount alone.
